Definition
The heart of any computing system is the Arithmetic Logic Unit or ALU..
INTRODUCTIONM
DEFINITION

ARITHMETIC LOGIC UNIT (ALU) - ALU is an integrated circuit that contains adders, counters, registers and logic circuits. The ALU performs math operations (adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing) and logic functions (AND, OR and NOT).
The ALU performs math operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.E
The four binary math operations are based on addition. The adder circuit is used to perform all 4 operations.
Let's begin the lesson on the 4 BIT ADDER.................................
LESSON MENU
An adder is designed specifically to add two, one bit binary numbers.
DISCUSSION
For example, a zero input on A and a zero input on B will produce a zero sum, zero carry.
Adding two ones will produce a zero sum, one carry.
This chart shows all 4 combinations of outputs possible from the addition of single digit binary numbers.
A half adder circuit is used to perform this operation.
A half adder circuit is used when the carry in is not important. A carry from a previous circuit will not be accepted.
In order to accept the carry from a previous circuit we must introduce the full adder circuit.
This chart shows all 8 combinations of outputs possible from the addition of single digit binary numbers in a full adder.
A full adder circuit is required when the carry in is important. A carry from a previous circuit will be accepted.

The full adder circuit adds binary numbers in serial or parallel. Let's look at a serial circuit first..
Two binary numbers are stored in registers A and B.
These two numbers were shifted in serially on the leading edge of the clock pulse..
The carry input is taken from the Q output of the flip-flop. The flip-flop changes as the carry out changes.
The CLR input resets the flip-flop before addition starts.m
On the leading edge of the first clock pulse, the first bit of each register shifts to the adder.
The CO keeps the flip-flop reset on the trailing edge of the clock pulse.
On the second clock pulse the ones are shifted to the adder.
The CO is high, setting the flip-flop on the trailing edge of the clock pulse.
On the third clock pulse, the third bits shift to the adder. Remember, the CI is now a one.
On the trailing edge of the clock pulse, the carry out is still one keeping the flip-flop set.
On the fourth clock pulse, the last bits are shifted to the adder. Remember, the CI is still one.
On the trailing edge of the clock pulse, the flip-flop remains set.
On the fifth clock pulse, zeros are shifted to the adder. The one on CI is also added.
On the trailing edge of the clock pulse, the flip-flop resets.
The serial adder required five clock pulses to add two, four bit binary numbers.
What are the contents of register C after 3 clock pulses?
At the first clock pulse the adder contains inputs A (1), B (1) and CI (0). Adding produces a sum of 0 and a carry of 1. Touch next to see more.
TRY AGAIN!
On the second pulse the adder contains inputs A (1), B (1) and CI (1). This produces a sum of 1 and a carry of 1. Touch next to see more.
At the third pulse the adder contains inputs A (0), B (1) and CI (1). Touch next to continue...
What is the output of the flip-flop after the third clock pulse?
The contents of the adder on the third clock pulse are 0, 1 and 1. The CO will determine the flip-flop's output.
TRY AGAIN!
The output of a flip-flop is never two bits. It can only be a 1 or a 0.

Note, the LSD adder is a half adder. If a full adder is used, the carry input is grounded.
The CO is used as the CI for the next adder.
The result from each adder is shifted to register C. Note, the last CO is used as the MSD digit in the register.
Let's add 1010 to 1110. Remember, all bits are added on one clock pulse.
When the clock pulse goes high, each pair of bits shift to its adder..
The result from each adder is then displayed in Register C.
